title: Stop Juggling Indexes: Use zip() to Loop Over Two Lists Together
excerpt: Loop over two lists together with zip() instead of juggling index numbers, and learn what happens when the lengths differ.

headings.text: When the Lists Are Different Lengths
Build a Dictionary From Two Lists
Unzip: Split Pairs Back Into Lists

html:
You have a list of names and a list of scores, and item 0 of one belongs with item 0 of the other. Looping over both at once is a very common need. The beginner's answer is to count positions by hand, and it works, but it is clumsy to write and easy to get wrong.

zip() pairs up items from two or more lists by position, so you can walk through them together in a single loop. This lesson shows how it works, what happens when the lists differ in length, and two handy tricks: building a dictionary and unzipping pairs back apart.

The Index-Juggling Way

Here is the approach without zip(). It loops over positions and looks up each list by index. In this code, len(names) counts the items, range produces the position numbers 0, 1, 2, and names[i] picks the item at position i:

names = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meena"]
scores = [82, 67, 91]

for i in range(len(names)):
    print(names[i], scores[i])
Asha 82
Ravi 67
Meena 91

It works, but you have to ask for the length, create position numbers, and index twice. Is there a way to say "go through these side by side"? There is, and it is called zip().

zip() Pairs Items Up

for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, score)
Asha 82
Ravi 67
Meena 91

Each time round the loop, zip() hands over one item from each list as a pair (a tuple, which is a fixed group of values in parentheses), and Python splits the pair into the two variable names. To see the pairs themselves, turn the result into a list:

print(list(zip(names, scores)))
[('Asha', 82), ('Ravi', 67), ('Meena', 91)]

Why the extra list()? Because zip() does not build the pairs immediately. It returns a kind of recipe that works out each pair only when the loop asks for it (programmers call this "lazy"). If you print it directly you only see that recipe, not the pairs:

print(zip(names, scores))
<zip object at 0x7f3a2c1b4d90>

(The number after at is a memory address and will be different on your machine.)

Three or More Lists

zip() accepts as many lists as you give it. Is there a limit of two? No:

passed = [True, True, False]

for name, score, ok in zip(names, scores, passed):
    print(name, score, ok)
Asha 82 True
Ravi 67 True
Meena 91 False

When the Lists Are Different Lengths

What happens to leftover items if one list is longer? zip() stops as soon as the shortest list runs out and quietly drops the rest:

print(list(zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"])))
[(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]

The 3 vanished without any warning, which can hide a real bug. If the lists are supposed to match, add the setting strict=True (available from Python 3.10) and Python will raise a ValueError, meaning "this value is not acceptable", instead of silently dropping data:

print(list(zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"], strict=True)))
ValueError: zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1

Build a Dictionary From Two Lists

Because zip() makes pairs, and a dictionary (which looks values up by a label) is made of key and value pairs, the two fit together. Can you build a dictionary straight from two lists? Yes: the names become the keys and the scores become the values:

score_by_name = dict(zip(names, scores))
print(score_by_name)
{'Asha': 82, 'Ravi': 67, 'Meena': 91}

Unzip: Split Pairs Back Into Lists

The trick also works in reverse. Put a * in front of a list of pairs and zip() regroups the first items together and the second items together:

pairs = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)]
letters, numbers = zip(*pairs)

print(letters)
print(numbers)
('a', 'b', 'c')
(1, 2, 3)

What does the star do here? In a function call, *pairs hands each pair to zip() as its own separate input, as if you had written zip(("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)). Regrouping those three pairs gives one tuple of letters and one tuple of numbers.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonZipFunction.ipynb.

Summary

  • zip(a, b) walks through lists side by side, giving one item from each on every turn.
  • It works with any number of lists: zip(a, b, c).
  • The result is lazy; wrap it in list() to see all the pairs at once.
  • It stops at the shortest list; use strict=True to raise a ValueError when lengths differ.
  • dict(zip(keys, values)) builds a dictionary from two lists.
  • zip(*pairs) reverses the process and splits pairs back into separate sequences.
